opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that we're still early, but early in a way that's genuinely exciting. When people hear "virtual cell," they sometimes imagine a perfect digital twin of a human cell that you can simulate end to end. That's not where we are, and frankly it's not what we need to be useful in the near term.

The way I'd frame near-term usefulness is: can a model predict how a cell will respond to a perturbation it hasn't seen before, well enough to change what experiment you run next? If you can knock down a gene, or add a drug, or combine perturbations, and the model tells you something non-obvious about the resulting cell state that then holds up at the bench, that's real value. It doesn't have to be perfect. It has to beat your intuition and beat the naive baselines.

And that last part matters a lot, because one of the sobering things the field has learned is that a lot of early models didn't convincingly beat very simple baselines, like predicting the mean expression change or using linear models. So I think the first milestone is just rigor: good benchmarks, held-out cell types, held-out perturbations, and being honest about whether we're actually generalizing or just memorizing the training distribution.

The data side is where I'm most optimistic. We can now generate perturbation data at a scale that was unthinkable a few years ago: single-cell readouts across millions of cells, many cell contexts, many genetic and chemical perturbations. That's the kind of substrate that lets these models get better in a compounding way, especially if you close the loop: the model proposes experiments, you run them, and the results feed back into training.

So in the near term, I see virtual cell models as hypothesis-ranking engines. They help you prioritize targets, predict combinations worth testing, and maybe flag liabilities earlier. Over a longer horizon, if they start to generalize across cell types and into contexts like patient-derived cells, that's when they could really reshape how we discover drugs. But we should earn that claim with data, not just assert it.

r001.rationale: The response says virtual cell models are still early, but also describes real near-term value as hypothesis-ranking engines. It does not say they need more time to mature before becoming fundamentally useful.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that virtual cell models are more useful today than most people expect, and less useful than the hype suggests. Both things are true at once.

Where they already work is in the narrow, well-measured regimes. If you've done a large perturbation screen in a cell line, a model trained on that data can do a reasonable job of predicting what an unseen gene knockout looks like in that same context. That's genuinely useful. It lets you prioritize which experiments to run next instead of brute-forcing every combination, and that compounds quickly when a single screen costs months and millions of dollars.

Where they break down is generalization. Move to a new cell type, a new tissue, a drug instead of a genetic perturbation, and performance drops off sharply. The models are mostly interpolating within the distribution of data they've seen. They're not yet learning cell biology in some deep mechanistic sense. And I'd say the field has been a little too quick to call a model a "virtual cell" when what it really is is a good perturbation-response predictor for one experimental setup.

The bottleneck isn't architecture, it's data. We have nothing like the internet for biology. The measurements we do have are noisy, batch-confounded, and heavily biased toward a handful of easy-to-grow cell lines. So I think the near-term value comes from a tight loop between the model and the lab, where the model tells you where its uncertainty is highest and you go generate exactly that data. That active learning flywheel is what I'd be investing in, more than any particular model.

So in the next two or three years, I'd expect these models to become standard tools for designing screens and triaging hypotheses. I wouldn't expect them to replace the experiment. The experiment is still the ground truth, and I think anyone who says otherwise hasn't tried to validate a prediction in a dish.

r001.rationale: The response describes current limitations and expects broader use in two or three years, but it also calls models genuinely useful today. It does not clearly state that they need time to mature before becoming fundamentally useful.

astra-6.text:
I think the near-term usefulness is going to be very task-specific. Can you predict how a particular cell type responds to a genetic perturbation or a drug? Can you use that prediction to choose a better next experiment? You don’t need a complete simulation of a cell for that to be valuable.

The distinction I’d make is between fitting the data we already have and predicting something genuinely new. If you change the biological context, does the model still work? Can it tell you when it’s uncertain? Those are much more useful tests than whether it generates something that looks like a plausible cell state.

So I’m optimistic about these models as tools for narrowing the search space and guiding experiments. The near-term opportunity is a loop where you make predictions, test them experimentally, and use those results to improve the model. That can accelerate discovery well before we have anything you’d call a comprehensive virtual cell.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes task-specific uses that can already guide experiments and accelerate discovery. It does not say virtual cell models need more time to mature before becoming fundamentally useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the near-term usefulness is going to be very task-specific. A virtual cell doesn’t need to simulate every molecule in a cell to be useful. If it can help you predict which perturbations to test, in which cell types, and under which conditions, that could make experimental biology much more efficient.

The distinction I’d make is between a model that produces plausible-looking cellular data and one that helps you discover something you didn’t already know. Can it predict what happens when you perturb a gene it hasn’t seen perturbed before? Can it generalize to a different cellular context? And does that prediction hold up when you do the experiment?

So I’m excited about a tight loop between models and experiments: use the model to prioritize experiments, generate the data, and use those results to improve the model. I think that’s where we’ll see useful progress well before we have anything you’d call a complete virtual cell.

r001.rationale: The response says virtual cell models can already be useful for specific tasks and enable progress before a complete virtual cell exists. It does not state that they need more time to mature before becoming fundamentally useful.
